title: LinkedIn Professional Network: Complete Architecture
description: Design a LinkedIn-scale professional network with N-degree graph traversal, People You May Know (PYMK), feed generation, and Who Viewed My Profile.

data.text: Design a professional social networking platform at LinkedIn scale. The platform serves 900+ million members across 200 countries. Unlike symmetric friendships or asymmetric Twitter follows, LinkedIn models professional connections with explicit degree relationships (1st: direct connection, 2nd: connected to your connection, 3rd: connected to your 2nd-degree). Core challenges include low-latency N-degree graph queries ("How you're connected"), People You May Know (PYMK) recommendation pipelines, member profile hydration, faceted job and people search, and privacy-aware "Who Viewed Your Profile" tracking.

terms.definition: 1st degree (direct mutual connection), 2nd degree (friends of friends), 3rd degree (friends of friends of friends). Determines visibility and messaging privileges.
Searching connection paths from both member A and member B simultaneously, meeting in the middle to find shared connections with O(b^(d/2)) complexity.
Graph recommendation engine computing triangle closing (shared mutual connections) and common attributes (schools, past companies, skills).
An event-driven analytics pipeline that logs profile visits, deduplicates within rolling windows, and renders viewer summaries while respecting privacy tiers.
LinkedIn-created real-time OLAP and key-value storage technologies built for sub-second analytical queries and high-throughput feature retrieval.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Member Profiles: Detailed work history, education, skills, endorsements, and certifications
Connection Graph: Send, accept, withdraw invitations; query 1st, 2nd, and 3rd degree connections
Connection Path: Display "How you are connected" (e.g., "You and Sarah both know David")
People You May Know (PYMK): Suggest relevant new connections based on mutual connections and career overlaps
Professional Feed: Posts, articles, company updates, and hiring announcements ranked by relevance
Who Viewed My Profile: Log profile visits and present aggregated analytics with viewer identity controls
Job & People Search: Search members and job postings with filters for location, company, and connection degree

data.title: Non-Functional Requirements
items: Scale: 900M+ registered members; 200M+ monthly active users; 100M+ connection graph edges
Graph Query Latency: <150ms P99 for 2nd-degree path lookups on profile views
Profile Loading Latency: <200ms P99 globally for fully hydrated profile pages
Availability: 99.99% for profile reading and feed browsing
Consistency: Strong consistency for connection state; eventual consistency for feed posts and search indexes

data.text: The architecture features a dedicated Distributed Graph Service to store and traverse connection edges, separated from relational member profile databases. An event streaming backbone (Kafka) drives asynchronous graph indexing, feed fan-out, and profile view analytics.

data.text: Graph Traversal: Bi-directional BFS for Mutual Connections
To find mutual connections and 2nd-degree paths between Member A and Member B without scanning millions of irrelevant edges, the Graph Service executes a bidirectional Breadth-First Search (BFS).

data.caption: Bidirectional BFS: Expanding 1st-degree connection sets from both sides to find common intersection nodes in O(b^(d/2)) time

faqs.question: How is "How You Are Connected" computed in under 150ms on profile view?
faqs.answer: Store 1st-degree connections as Redis Sets (`conn:member_id`). When Member A views Member B, the Graph Service executes `SINTER conn:A conn:B` to find the set intersection of mutual connections. Because set intersection runs on in-memory integer arrays, it completes in <5ms even for members with thousands of connections.

faqs.question: How does People You May Know (PYMK) scale to 900M users?
faqs.answer: PYMK is not computed on the fly during page load. An offline distributed batch/streaming pipeline (Apache Spark / Flink) runs daily triangle-closing algorithms over the graph. It generates candidate pools scored by mutual connections, past shared companies, and common universities, caching the top 100 suggestions in a distributed key-value store (Venice).

faqs.question: How does "Who Viewed My Profile" preserve member privacy modes?
faqs.answer: When Member A visits Member B, a `ProfileViewEvent` is published to Kafka containing A's identity and their privacy setting (`FULL_NAME`, `SEMI_PRIVATE` e.g., "Someone in the Internet Industry in San Francisco", or `PRIVATE`). The analytics ingestion worker masks the viewer details according to their preference before writing to Apache Pinot and notifying Member B.

faqs.question: Why does LinkedIn use Document Sharding for member profiles?
faqs.answer: Member profiles are partitioned by `member_id` across the distributed document store (Espresso). Since 99% of profile reads query a specific individual, all profile subsections (work experience, education, endorsements) reside on the same database partition, enabling single-roundtrip retrieval.

faqs.question: How are degree-filtered search queries ("2nd-degree connections who work at Google") processed?
faqs.answer: The search indexer embeds graph membership tokens or runs post-search graph filtering. Galene (LinkedIn's search engine) intersects inverted index postings for "Company: Google" with the searcher's 1st/2nd degree connection ID bitsets, producing fast, graph-aware candidate matches.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Bi-directional BFS and in-memory Set intersections (Redis SINTER) make 2nd-degree path search sub-10ms
PYMK graph triangle-closing is computed asynchronously in batch pipelines and pre-warmed into fast key-value caches
Who Viewed My Profile uses Kafka and Apache Pinot for real-time OLAP metrics with privacy masking
Profile datastores shard by Member ID so all personal resume data is fetched in a single network hop
Search engines blend inverted index document matching with in-memory graph degree bitsets
data.takeaway: LinkedIn's system architecture excels at real-time professional graph queries by pairing in-memory adjacency sets for immediate 1st/2nd degree lookups with asynchronous batch engines for computationally intensive recommendations.
